common_name: Contender Bush Bean (Popular Early Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil; Contender is a widely grown early bush snap bean prized for producing a full crop in a short window, making it ideal for succession planting through the season.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Contender is a longtime favorite early bush snap bean, valued for reaching harvest size faster than most other bush beans and tolerating somewhat cooler soil at planting than many varieties, giving Gulf South gardeners an early start on the bean season. Its round, meaty, stringless pods have good flavor and hold quality well for a short window before toughening, making regular harvest important. Because the whole crop tends to mature at once, Contender is an excellent choice for succession sowing every two to three weeks to maintain a steady bean harvest through summer, and for canning or freezing a full batch at one time.

common_name: Snowbird Pea (Early Dwarf Shelling Pea for Southern Gardens)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Snowbird is an early, dwarf shelling pea bred to mature quickly before hot weather ends the pea season in Southern gardens.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Snowbird is a short, self-supporting dwarf shelling pea bred to mature very quickly, an important trait in the Gulf South where the cool-season pea window is narrow before summer heat arrives and stops pod production. Its compact vines need little to no staking, and the concentrated, early harvest lets gardeners get a pea crop in before spring warms up too much. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking regularly to encourage the plant to keep flowering during its short productive window.

common_name: Cascadia Snap Pea (Disease-Resistant Oregon State-Bred Snap Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Cascadia is an Oregon State University-bred snap pea noted for disease resistance and reliable production on compact vines.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing light support such as netting or twiggy brush for the vines. Cascadia was bred at Oregon State University and is valued for good resistance to powdery mildew and other common pea diseases, along with sweet, crisp, edible pods on compact, easy-to-support vines that produce reliably even in less-than-ideal spring weather. Its snap-pea type pods are eaten whole, pod and all, once they fill out but before the peas inside become starchy. Harvest regularly once pods reach full size to encourage continued production through the relatively short Gulf South pea season.

common_name: Sugar Bon Pea (AAS-Winning Dwarf Snap Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Sugar Bon is an All-America Selections winner bred as a dwarf snap pea that needs little to no staking while still producing sweet, crisp pods.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Sugar Bon, an All-America Selections winner, combines the sweet, crisp, whole-pod-edible quality of snap peas with an unusually compact, dwarf vine that needs little to no staking, making it a convenient choice for small gardens, containers, or gardeners who want to skip trellising. It sets pods heavily and matures quickly, an advantage in the Gulf South's relatively short cool-season pea window before summer heat arrives. Harvest pods once they fill out but are still tender and glossy, picking every couple of days to encourage the vine to keep producing through its productive window.
